craft_claim: Rhyme and phonetic patterning raise perceived truth and aptness, so sound in the lyrical tone carries epistemic weight rather than merely pleasing the ear.

supporting_evidence.note: Rhyming aphorisms were judged more truthful and more apt than semantically equivalent non-rhyming versions; the effect survived even when the original rhyme words were replaced.
The authors frame the effect as a heuristic in which the sound of a statement is misattributed to its sense.

counterevidence.note: The mechanism is a misattribution of fluency, not a reliable guide to truth; rhyme can make a false or thin statement persuasive.

scope: Aphorism, epigram, closing lines, headlines, and any short cadenced assertion where sound and sense can be aligned.
exceptions: Technical, legal, or evidentiary writing where sound-based persuasion is a defect rather than a feature.
Audiences primed to distrust rhetorical form.
